introduction_markdown:
**General Certificate of Education (GCE) Board - General Certificate of Education Examination. Philosophy 2 (0790), Paper 2 (Philosophical Culture), ADVANCED LEVEL, June 2021. Duration: three hours.**

Candidates are expected to answer FOUR (04) questions chosen from the three sections imperatively (that is, with questions taken from each of the three sections).

Each essay must contain:
- An introduction = 5 marks
- A thesis = 7 marks
- An antithesis = 6 marks
- A synthesis = 3 marks
- A conclusion = 4 marks

Each question carries 25 marks.

Candidates are reminded of the necessity for good English and orderly presentation of material.
incertitudes: Règle de choix : la page de garde dit « answer FOUR (04) questions chosen from the three sections imperatively » (quatre questions au total, prises dans les trois sections). Le sujet ne dit pas explicitement « au moins une par section » ; cela est déduit de « imperatively » et du format des autres années. `regles_choix` porte le minimum, une règle `parmi 1 sur 2` par section (Section One : questions 1-2 ; Section Two : questions 3-4 ; Section Three : questions 5-6) ; la règle « 4 questions en tout » n'est pas exprimable et est recopiée dans `introduction_markdown`. Les deux sous-sections de la Section Three (Descartes, texte de philosophie africaine) sont comptées comme une seule section de deux questions ; le sujet ne dit pas si un candidat peut traiter les questions 5 et 6 à la fois.

Points : chaque question est imprimée « 25 marks » (4 x 25 = 100). Les critères de la page de garde (introduction 5, thèse 7, antithèse 6, synthèse 3, conclusion 4 = 25) s'appliquent aux dissertations (questions 1 à 4) ; les questions de textes (5 et 6) ont leurs propres points par sous-question.

Aucun corrigé officiel : les corrigés sont des réponses modèles rédigées de mémoire, sans accès à une source. Les auteurs et positions cités (Sophistes, Socrate, Kierkegaard, Nkrumah, Nyerere, Gyekye, Wiredu, Mbiti, Césaire, Fanon, Descartes, Hume, Kant...) sont ceux de l'histoire de la philosophie établie, sans citation littérale ni numéro de page ; les dates et faits historiques cités sont donnés dans leurs grandes lignes. À faire relire par un enseignant de philosophie avant mise en avant.

Sujet scanné (3 pages) avec filigrane gcerevision.com et bandeau publicitaire sans incidence sur la lecture ; aucune figure. Page de garde vérifiée : ADVANCED LEVEL, Philosophy 2, Paper 2 (Philosophical Culture), code 0790, JUNE 2021, trois heures.

questions.enonce_markdown:
"The Leap of Faith" is the turning point in Kierkegaard's existentialism. Justify this view.

(25 marks)
questions.corrige_markdown:
**Introduction (5 marks).** Soren Kierkegaard (1813-1855), a Danish thinker, is generally regarded as a founder of existentialism. Against Hegel's system and the comfortable Christianity of his time, he maintained that truth for an existing individual must be lived, chosen and personally appropriated. He speaks of a "leap" in Fear and Trembling (signed Johannes de Silentio) and in the Concluding Unscientific Postscript (signed Johannes Climacus); the fixed phrase "leap of faith" is rather that of later commentators. To justify the view set means to show that this leap is the decisive moment of his thought. The problem is whether the leap is really the turning point of his existentialism, or only one element of it.

**Thesis: the leap is the turning point (7 marks).**

*The limits of reason.* For Kierkegaard no objective proof can establish the central claim of Christianity, that God became man in time. Reason meets an "absolute paradox" and objective uncertainty remains. Faith therefore cannot be the conclusion of an argument; it is a decision of the whole person, made with passion and risk, across the gap that reason cannot close. This is the leap. It marks the turning point from a philosophy that tries to understand existence from outside (Hegel's speculative system) to a philosophy that takes existence as lived from inside.

*Abraham.* In Fear and Trembling Abraham is ordered to sacrifice his son Isaac. He acts "by virtue of the absurd", beyond the universal moral rule, in what Kierkegaard calls a teleological suspension of the ethical. The tragic hero can be understood and justified by the community; the knight of faith stands alone before God, with no rational justification to offer. The story shows the leap as the highest act of the individual.

*The stages of existence.* Kierkegaard describes an aesthetic stage (life of pleasure and possibility), an ethical stage (duty and commitment) and a religious stage (relation to God). One does not pass from one stage to the next by logical deduction, as in Hegel's dialectic of mediation, but by a choice, an "either/or" (Either/Or, 1843). The leap to the religious stage completes this movement. It expresses what is central to existentialism: individual freedom and responsibility, and the priority of existing over systems.

**Antithesis: the leap is not the only turning point (6 marks).**

First, Kierkegaard's existentialism rests on several other pillars: the single individual standing before God, the claim that "truth is subjectivity", anxiety understood as the dizziness of freedom (The Concept of Anxiety, 1844), despair as the sickness unto death (1849), and the attack on the crowd and on the established church of Christendom. One may argue that subjectivity, not the leap, is the foundation, and that the leap is the religious application of it.

Second, the leap is open to serious criticism. If faith is beyond reason, it is hard to tell faith from fanaticism: anyone could claim, like Abraham, a divine command that no one can examine. Critics speak of irrationalism or fideism. Kierkegaard's reply is that faith is a paradox lived with risk, not a proof, but the objection remains.

Third, later existentialists kept Kierkegaard's themes of freedom, choice and anguish but rejected the leap. Sartre, an atheist, makes the individual alone responsible for creating his meaning. Camus, in The Myth of Sisyphus, calls the leap a kind of philosophical suicide, a refusal to face the absurd honestly. Jaspers kept a "philosophical faith" that is not the Kierkegaardian leap. So existentialism as a movement can exist without the leap.

**Synthesis (3 marks).** The two views can be reconciled by distinguishing Kierkegaard's own religious existentialism from existentialism in general. In the first, the leap is the turning point, the culmination of subjectivity, anxiety and choice. In the second, the common core is the primacy of individual existence and freedom, of which the leap is one possible (religious) expression.

**Conclusion (4 marks).** The view is therefore justified for Kierkegaard's own thought: the leap is where his critique of rational systems, his account of the stages and his conception of the free individual meet and are completed. It is not justified if it means that all existentialism depends on a leap of faith, since atheistic existentialists build on freedom and the absurd without it.
